title: Timms says Pip review being published today will ‘rehumanise’ benefit – UK politics live
summary: Some recommendations expected to clash with those of Milburn’s recent report into Neets

blocks.text:
Some recommendations expected to clash with those of Milburn’s recent report into Neets

  • UK disability benefit cuts ‘risk worsening youth destitution’

Andy Burnham has made a point of paying less attention to the legacy mainstream media than his predecessors, and giving more access to social media influencers. He may be having second thoughts.

During his Commons statement yesterday, a Tory MP complained about Burnham letting the TikTok star Luke Hamnett into No 10 to recreate the Hugh Grant dance scene from the film Love Actually.

Would I use that language? Absolutely not. Do I want to hear that kind of language anywhere, wherever it is? No, I don’t.

I think it’s right that the prime minister talks to lots of different people and lots of different media outlets.

I’m sure you wouldn’t want me saying that I can control, or the prime minister should control, what broadcasters say outside No 10.

At a time when Trump, Xi and Putin are projecting power on the world stage, and people across Britain are anxious about the future, this looks extremely unserious

Being relatable doesn’t mean treating the public as though they are children who need entertaining.

Last week’s Milburn review called for Pip to be scrapped for younger claimants, and for the health element of universal credit to be replaced by an additional cost allowance, part of a wider network of job-based help for this age group.

The shock among the organisations which had contributed to Timms was palpable, says Patrick [Butler, the Guardian’s social affairs editor]. “The idea that you basically blow up Pip for younger people took a lot of groups by surprise.”
